sources.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security

items.title: A Mass Fridge Hack in France, and a Password the Calendar Supplies
items.body:
Ars Technica reports that a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction.

The same reporting flags a security detail that is hard to shrug off: until recently, Danfoss controllers used a credential that changes each day — and the password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A password the calendar and a downloadable firmware can produce for you is not really protecting anything. The only thing standing between a stranger and the equipment is that they have to read the manual.

sources.title: Fires Arrive in the Amazon Rainforest

items.title: A Drought-Primed Amazon, and Smoke Over Manaus
items.body:
A drought accompanying El Niño has left the Amazon rainforest primed to burn, and scientists say the region has entered the early stages of what they think will be a long and severe fire season.

By October 12, heavy smoke had socked in Manaus, the capital of the Brazilian state of Amazonas, according to NASA. The expectation is not a passing bad week: the scientists quoted describe a season they think will run long and severe, and say it is only now getting started.

sources.title: Fraternity culture under scrutiny in wake of Cornell allegations

items.title: Cornell Suspends Fraternity Parties; Faculty Plan a No-Confidence Vote
items.body:
PBS NewsHour reports that the fallout from sexual assault allegations at Cornell University is moving on two tracks. Faculty members plan to introduce a resolution of no confidence in how leadership handled an alleged gang rape at a fraternity. The university has suspended fraternity parties through the academic year and committed to a thorough review of fraternity life.

The two responses aim at different targets — one at the administration's handling of the complaint, the other at fraternity social life as a whole.

sources.title: Q&A: The “collision” between AI, your brain, and society

discussion.body: So's own account of how learning works cuts against defaulting to the tool: he says the evidence shows our ability to learn gets dramatically better when we wrestle with material, work through initial failures and keep iterating.

Anthropic's analysis found that about half of queries from college students were low-effort requests for simple answers. That measures demand for easy answers, not what using them does to anyone's thinking.

items.title: The Case That Relying on AI Atrophies Thinking
items.body:
MIT professor Eric So argues in his new book, The Collision: What AI Does to Us, that heavy use of AI can lead to a kind of cognitive atrophy, in which people fail to develop and retain essential thinking skills.

Note the hedging: heavy use, can. This is a risk claim about what happens over time, not a verdict that anyone who asks a chatbot a question gets dumber. It does invite the obvious follow-up — which parts of thinking are worth refusing to hand over.

sources.title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam

items.title: Epic Says It "Vibe Coded" a New Games Launcher
items.body:
Epic is putting out a publicly available preview build of a rewritten Epic Games Launcher, and its announcement makes a joke of the whole enterprise: programming is hard, so instead of doing that, the company says, it vibe coded a new launcher that is way faster and more responsive than the current one.

It's the kind of line that gets a laugh and covers a serious bet. The rebuild arrives nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own game store and launcher, and the company is presenting vibe coding — its own phrase for the work — as the thing that gives it an edge over Valve.

The speed is the part to hold loosely. "Faster and more responsive" is Epic's account of its own rebuild, and responsiveness is exactly the kind of claim a vendor can assert and only users can confirm.

sources.title: APOD: 2026 October 15 – The Milky Way over Manhattan

items.title: How the Milky Way Shows Up Over Manhattan
items.body:
NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day is a photograph of the Milky Way over Manhattan, a sky where, as the accompanying explanation notes, the city lights outshine the stars.

The picture works because of the band it is taken in. The astrophotographer's setup blocks most of the city's light pollution, and the explanation offers a pleasingly specific reason why: old incandescent bulbs and some neon lights are still bright in the near-infrared, but fluorescent and LED bulbs are not.

That makes light pollution less like a single dimmer switch than like a set of bulbs. It depends on the wavelength you're looking at and on what the fixtures are made of, which means the same city glow that hides the sky from one camera may barely register in another.

sources.title: Attorney for banned outlets on legal fight over White House press access

items.title: A Judge Orders the White House to Restore Access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico
items.body:
A federal judge has once again ordered the White House to restore access for three news organizations that President Trump banned last month over their coverage of his administration. CNN, MS NOW and Politico get full access while their legal challenge moves forward.

The word to notice is "again." A judge ordering the same thing twice suggests the first order didn't settle the matter. And "while their legal challenge moves forward" matters just as much — this is interim relief, not a ruling on whether the White House may shut out outlets over coverage it dislikes. That question is still being litigated.

sources.title: My own security system flagged me, a Black woman, as an animal

discussion.body: The comparison is the strongest thing in the account. The household comes with a control subject, and he has never once drawn the label.
It's still two incidents in one yard. That's enough to justify hard questions about how the system was built and tuned, not enough to put a number on how often this happens to whom.
Fair — though a rate wouldn't capture the direction anyway. What unsettles is that the person the system kept ignoring is the one who looks nothing like the person it kept flagging.

items.title: A Home Security System Kept Labeling Its Black Owner an Animal
items.body:
Writing in The Conversation Canada, a Black woman describes the first time her home security system flagged her as an animal: she was sitting at her patio table with her morning coffee. A few months later it happened again, as she walked across the yard to catch the afternoon sun. Her husband, who is white, has never drawn that label from the system.

Two incidents and one comparison make an anecdote, not a rate. But the asymmetry is the part worth sitting with. A classifier that works for most people is invisible to most people; the ones who see it fail are the ones it fails on, and from inside one house the pattern stops looking like bad luck.

sources.title: Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest

items.title: A Toronto Court Hears How $4.5 Million Went to the Self-Described 'Crypto King'
items.body: Real estate developer Sacha Singh told a Toronto court he gave Aiden Pleterski more than $4.5 million to trade in foreign exchange and cryptocurrency, CBC reports. Singh's figure is larger than that of any of the 11 investors called so far as Crown witnesses at Pleterski's fraud trial. Whether a verdict ever settles the question, the number does some work on its own: one developer's cheque outweighs the testimony of every other investor the Crown has put on the stand to this point.

sources.title: In the northern Appalachian Mountains, warmer weather is making alpine regions greener

discussion.body: Worth separating two things here. A greening signal gathered from orbit is a statement about how the summits look from above; 'trees are marching uphill' would be a statement about which species actually moved in.

The researchers do name the stakes in their own terms: what a greener summit means for the plants that live where cold and wind are too extreme for trees to survive. That is the question the greening trend hands them.

items.title: Why Trees Stop at the Alpine Zone, and Why a Greener Summit Is Worth Watching
items.body: Climb toward a northern Appalachian peak and the trees run out before the summit does. They get shorter as you gain altitude, then vanish at the alpine zone, where the climate is harsh enough that the plants cling close to the ground rather than stand up in trunks and branches. That strip — call it an island in the sky — is what makes the next finding interesting. Researchers writing in The Conversation Canada used 41 years of satellite imagery of mountains across the northeastern United States and Québec's Gaspé Peninsula, and they report that these summits are slowly greening. A summit that turns greener is a summit where something is finding a foothold.

sources.title: How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections

items.title: Data Centres Are Drawing the Same Objection From Both US Parties
items.body: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data-centre development amid a growing backlash across the United States, the BBC reports. Opposition that cuts across the usual party divide is its own kind of story: on an infrastructure question this size, the fight is not shaping up as the familiar partisan split.

sources.title: Indonesian VIP prison scandal exposes inequality across Southeast Asia

items.title: A Luxury Cell in an Indonesian Prison, and a Regional Grievance About Money
items.body: Luxury accommodation has been uncovered at an Indonesian prison, Deutsche Welle reports, reigniting concerns in Southeast Asia about preferential treatment for wealthy convicts. The fittings are the scandal; the complaint they revive is about what money can still buy after conviction.

sources.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator James Cody Bryant indicted by grand jury

items.title: A Grand Jury in Washington State Indicts an Alleged Co-Conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge Shooting
items.body: A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. CBC reports that the indictment charges 30-year-old James Bryant with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, and that it means prosecutors have probable cause to pursue the case. That is a finding of probable cause, not a conviction — the case now proceeds rather than concludes.

sources.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping

items.title: India Asks Moscow and Kyiv to Keep Black Sea Shipping Safe
items.body: New Delhi wants Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea, where attacks are putting Indian seafarers at risk, Deutsche Welle reports. The appeal puts the safety of India's own crews at the centre of the argument over a waterway it does not control — a reminder that a war's shipping disruptions are felt well beyond the two countries fighting it.

sources.title: Triplet of ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Hints at What Dark Matter Is — and Isn’t

items.title: Three Galaxies 65 Million Light-Years Away That Barely Glow
items.body: About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don't look quite right. They aren't whirlpools bursting with light but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” Yale University astrophysicist Michael Keim told Quanta Magazine. A galaxy that is hard to see is not necessarily a small thing — the faintness here is the feature that makes the trio worth a second look.

sources.title: Aboard an icebreaker, a writer got a closer look at the Arctic's 'Sea Change'

items.title: The Arctic's Opening Lanes and the Competition That Follows
items.body: As polar ice melts in the Arctic, shipping lanes are opening up, and the region is becoming a new zone of superpower competition, NPR reports. Writer Rana Foroohar, who got a closer look from aboard an icebreaker, lays out the stakes in her book Sea Change. Melting ice is usually framed as a climate story, and it is one — but it is also a story about who gets to use the water that appears in its place.

sources.title: Major projects CEO faces B.C. First Nations’ frustrations over lack of consultations

items.title: B.C. First Nations Push for National Consultation Standards on Major Projects
items.body: First Nations in British Columbia are calling on Ottawa to set national standards for Indigenous consultations on major projects. They say they were given limited time to review the proposal.

sources.title: Doug Ford says Republicans might ‘pull the carpet’ under Trump if midterms are lost

items.title: Doug Ford Suggests Democrats Could Flip Congress in U.S. Midterms
items.body: As the midterm elections draw closer, Doug Ford is dipping a toe into American politics. He stated that Democrats might be able to flip the Senate and the House of Representatives.

sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology

discussion.body: Proposing patches in minutes is a striking claim for a security operations team.
It's OpenAI's own description of Block's work. The useful question is how those proposed patches perform under real incident pressure.
Fair—speed and correctness are different benchmarks.

items.title: OpenAI Says Block's Security Team Uses AI to Propose Patches in Minutes
items.body: OpenAI says Block is building AI-powered security with its technology. According to OpenAI, Block's security team investigates threats faster and proposes patches in minutes. That is a vendor's account of a customer's results, not an independent evaluation.

sources.title: Variety’s 2026 Artisans to Watch: ‘Obsession’ Makeup Head, ‘Project Hail Mary’ Animation Supervisor, ‘La Bola Negra’ Composer and More

items.title: Variety Reports a 2026 Cinema Comeback Spanning Blockbusters and Low-Budget Films
items.body: Variety reports that in 2026, moviegoers came back to cinemas, packing theaters for blockbusters such as “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary,” “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “Toy Story 5,” “Michael,” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” as well as low-budget films like “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” The list includes both big-budget sequels and smaller films.
